title: Up or down by a percentage

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the bar's end sliding past 100% for a rise and back from it for a cut, so the new amount is the old one stretched or squeezed by the multiplier, when you add the percentage to 100% or take it away and divide by 100.
interactive.title: Up or down by a percentage
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens on a percentage bar, the old amount bracketed above it as 100% and the new amount below it, with an end you can drag, some screens showing an idea and the rest asking you to try it.
interactive.ignores: The amounts (£150, 40 A, 230 V, 30 m and the rest) are example values, chosen to show the method.

numbers.label: 40 A up 15%: 40 × 1.15 = 46 A, where adding 15 would give 55 A, in step 2
£60 down 20%: 60 × 0.8 = £48, while 60 × 0.2 = £12 is the part taken off, in step 4
50 m stretched or squeezed: 50 × 1.2 = 60 m and 50 × 0.85 = 42.5 m, in step 5
£120 with 25% off: 75% is left, 120 × 0.75 = £90, in step 7
30 m up 150%: 250%, so 30 × 2.5 = 75 m, where 150% of 30 m is 45 m, in step 9

explain.text:
To raise an amount by a percentage, you can add the percentage to 100% and find that percentage of the amount.[^1] Up 20% ends at 120%, which is 1.2 as a decimal, so £150 up 20% is 150 × 1.2 = £180 in one step. That 1.2 is the multiplier. A cut works the same way with the percentage taken from 100%, so down 15% leaves 85% and the multiplier is 0.85, and a single multiplier does a cut in one step too.[^2] A multiplier over 1 stretches an amount, and one under 1 squeezes it.

The slips to watch are adding the percentage as if it were a number, which makes £150 up 20% come to £170 instead of £180, and stopping at the change itself, the £30 on its own. Dividing by 10 instead of 100 carries over as well, since reading 3% as 0.3 makes a 3% rise × 1.3 instead of × 1.03.[^3] Up 100% doubles an amount, so up 150% ends at 250%, × 2.5, while 150% of it is only × 1.5.

**Add a rise to 100%, or take a cut from 100%, and divide by 100 for the multiplier. Up 20% is × 1.2 and down 15% is × 0.85, one step on a calculator.**

practice.text:
**Rule of thumb:** Add a rise to 100%, or take a cut from 100%, then divide by 100 for the multiplier.[^1] A rise multiplies by more than 1 and a cut by less than 1, which makes a quick check.

**Worked example:** A 230 V supply drops 4% along a cable run. 100% − 4% = 96%, so the multiplier is 0.96, and 230 × 0.96 = 220.8 V. As a check, 4% of 230 V is 9.2 V, and 230 − 9.2 = 220.8.

**Common mistakes**
- Adding the percentage as a number. £150 up 20% is not £170. 20% of £150 is £30, so it comes to £180.
- Stopping at the change. 60 × 0.2 = £12 is the 20% taken off, and 60 × 0.8 = £48 is the price that is left.
- Dividing by 10 instead of 100. Up 3% is × 1.03, while × 1.3 would be up 30%.[^3]
- Mixing up a rise and a cut. Up 8% is × 1.08, and 8% off is × 0.92.
- Reading up 150% as 150% of. Up 150% ends at 250%, so 30 m becomes 30 × 2.5 = 75 m, not 45 m.
